summary.text: The foreword states that ethical research is vital to WHO's work and that strong ethical standards must be understood and applied by researchers and sponsors, especially in low-resource settings. It presents case-based group discussion as an effective way to learn to apply ethical principles and is signed by WHO's Assistant Director-General for information, evidence and research.

sections.title: Page 13

summary.text: The introduction explains that the casebook contains 64 case studies, each raising a hard ethical issue in planning, reviewing or conducting health research, especially international studies. It is meant to aid teaching, from short workshops to degree courses, and includes a facilitator's guide. It notes growing international concern that health research can both benefit and harm the communities studied.

summary.text: Notes that risk of harm is greater where participants are poor, illiterate or lack other access to care, and that all WHO-supported research is reviewed by WHO ethics committees. It explains that the committee secretariat has long used case studies in its training, with experts from the Harvard School of Public Health, and that the cases grew out of more than a decade of joint workshops.

It cites the Declaration of Helsinki among source materials.

summary.text: Weighs starting with a case versus a lecture and advises on finding a good starting point for discussion. It suggests splitting large groups into small groups of six to eight for 20–30 minutes, with the facilitator moving between them. It also encourages challenging the reasoning of participants who share the facilitator's views.

summary.text: Opens the facilitator's guide to the chapters of the Arabic edition of the WHO Casebook on ethical issues in international health research.
